fixes.explanation: Silver, friend. Joseph tells his steward to put each man's silver in the mouth of his sack, along with all the food they can carry. Pharaoh had put Joseph over the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:41), and this isn't the first time he has had silver slipped back into their sacks (Genesis 42:25). He's making a habit of it.

Joseph did receive a signet ring, and Pharaoh, Egypt's king, was the one who gave it to him (Genesis 41:42). But the text never puts a ring in any sack. Joseph's order is for his cup, the silver one, in the youngest one's sack. The ring just isn't part of this plan.

Pharaoh really did put a gold chain around Joseph's neck (Genesis 41:42). It's a fine piece of jewelry, but it never goes into a sack in this story. What Joseph has the steward put in the youngest one's sack is his silver cup. The chain isn't part of this plan.

Right, and that's a big question. Joseph tells the steward to ask, "Why have you repaid good with evil?" The steward is to say it as soon as he overtakes them, and then he adds the part about the cup. That's a loaded line to get from a man who just rode up behind your donkeys.

The brothers offer that deal, but the steward doesn't take all of it. He says, "As you say…" and then changes the terms. "…only the one who is found with the cup will be my slave, and the rest of you shall be free of blame." So the rest of them aren't made slaves.

Oldest first. The steward searches, "…beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest…" That means Benjamin's sack is the last one searched. I bet that felt like a very long search for the brothers.

The youngest is where the search ends, not where it starts. The steward goes "…beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest…" Benjamin is the youngest, so his sack is the last one searched, and that's where the cup is found (Genesis 44:12).

Yes, they do. After the cup is found, they all tear their clothes, load their donkeys, and go back to the city. I think the torn clothes show how hard the news hit them. They had already set out for home, and now they turn around.
They do go back, all of them. The text says, "Then they all tore their clothes, loaded their donkeys, and returned to the city." They had already set out for home, and now they turn around together.

Dead is what they told Joseph. They said, "The boy’s brother is dead." Joseph is that brother, and he is standing right in front of them while they say it (Genesis 43:29). They don't know who they're talking to (Genesis 42:8).
Nobody says blind. The brothers told Joseph, "The boy’s brother is dead." That's the word Judah reports. Blindness doesn't come up anywhere in what Judah says.

They did say that. Judah reports that they told Joseph, "The boy cannot leave his father. If he were to leave, his father would die." That's what they told him back when Joseph asked to see the boy. Now Judah is bringing it up again.

They did warn him, so this one is true. Judah says they told Joseph, "The boy cannot leave his father. If he were to leave, his father would die." He's walking Joseph back through that earlier conversation.
No river in Jacob's words. He said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces." Judah is passing along what his father said. This is a sad moment, and I think it's meant to be heard slowly.

That's it. Judah says, "…your servant guaranteed the boy’s safety to my father…" He told his father he would bear the guilt all his life if he didn't return the boy. So when he asks to stay, he's offering himself in Benjamin's place.

That's the big ask. Judah says, "Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers." He offers himself so Benjamin can go home. I think that's a real turn from the Judah who once suggested selling Joseph (Genesis 37:26-27).

Misery is the word. Judah says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." He's talking about his father if the boy isn't with them. That's why he asks Joseph to keep him instead (Genesis 44:33).
Anger isn't the word. Judah says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." The word he uses is misery, and it's his father who would be overwhelmed by it.
Shame isn't the word Judah uses. He says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." The word is misery, and it's about what would overwhelm his father.
